cues.text: Voices in a Village Garden

Born around 1412 at Domrémy in the borderlands of Champagne, Joan — Jeanne d'Arc, known to her contemporaries as la Pucelle , "the Maid" — grew up the daughter of a modest, unimpoverished peasant farmer.

Her village had remained loyal to the French crown throughout the bitter civil conflict dividing France between the Armagnac party of the young King Charles VII and the Burgundian faction allied with occupying English forces.
At thirteen, Joan began experiencing what she consistently described as visions and voices.
She attributed them to St. Michael the Archangel and to Sts. Catherine and Margaret.
Over the following years, they instructed her with growing urgency to aid the French king and deliver France from English domination.
Convincing a Skeptical Court

Against every reasonable expectation for an illiterate teenage girl of no rank or military training, Joan managed, through sheer persistence, to secure an audience first with a local garrison commander.
She eventually met Charles VII himself, convincing the initially doubtful prince and his advisors of the genuineness of her mission.
Reportedly, according to persistent tradition, she identified him correctly despite his having disguised himself among his own courtiers to test her.
After subjecting Joan to further theological examination to rule out demonic deception, Charles agreed to send her, at about seventeen, to join the relief effort.
The effort sought to relieve the besieged city of Orléans , and Charles equipped her with armor and a banner bearing the names of Jesus and Mary.
The Siege of Orléans Lifted
Joan's arrival at Orléans in 1429 transformed the morale of a French army that had endured months of demoralizing siege.
Leading troops into battle behind her banner, she inspired decisive engagements that forced the English to abandon the siege within only nine days.
The reversal was so sudden and complete that it struck contemporaries on both sides as something close to miraculous.
Joan pressed her advantage further still, urging Charles to proceed at once to Reims for his formal coronation.
Achieved on July 17, 1429, it was an event of immense symbolic importance that Joan herself regarded as the true fulfillment of her God-given mission.
Capture and a Trial Designed to Convict
Joan's fortunes turned sharply the following year.
Attempting to relieve the besieged town of Compiègne, she was captured by Burgundian forces in May 1430 and sold to the English.

Recognizing her immense symbolic value, they resolved to try her for heresy — a strategy calculated both to eliminate a formidable adversary and to discredit the legitimacy of the king whose crown she had helped secure.
Her trial was conducted at Rouen under the presiding judge, Bishop Pierre Cauchon, a committed partisan of the English cause.
It subjected Joan to months of relentless interrogation designed to trap her into either heresy or a confession undermining her divine mission.

The surviving trial record shows a defendant of remarkable composure, simplicity, and good sense, who repeatedly outmaneuvered her judges' attempts at entrapment while refusing to answer certain questions she judged unfair or improperly framed.
Burned at the Stake

Convicted as a relapsed heretic, Joan was burned at the stake in the marketplace of Rouen on May 30, 1431, only nineteen years old, protesting her innocence and the truth of her voices to the very end.

Witnesses recorded that she called repeatedly on the name of Jesus as the flames rose, and that even some among the English soldiers present were visibly moved, one reportedly declaring afterward that they had burned a saint.
Legacy
A formal Church inquiry was conducted between 1449 and 1456 at the request of Charles VII.
Drawing on testimony from over a hundred witnesses, it declared Joan's original trial null and void, formally rehabilitating her memory within a generation of her death.
Beatified in 1909 and canonized in 1920, Joan of Arc remains one of the most extraordinary figures in the whole of Christian history.
She was an illiterate peasant girl who, trusting completely in voices no one else could hear, altered the course of a war and secured a kingdom's rightful crown.
She was burned as a heretic by the very institution that would one day raise her to its altars as a saint.
